Well, it's certainly a rapidly expanding industry. My company had to close shop after the 2008 financial crisis, but reopened in 2013. Find a chem lab, or an engineering firm, or whoever makes nano-blood-widgets near your school; and try to do something there. It depends on the program the school you're at/looking at has and what the industry looks like in your area. Where I'm at, we have a really great biotechnology program that gives you loads of hands-on experience, teaches you loads of techniques, and actually prepares you for entering the biotechnology industry. Also, the school is about half an hour away from one of the largest biotech/biopharmaceutical hubs in the country. Our program has a 90+% job placement rate (within 6 months of graduation), and that's just with a minor in biotechnology.

But in general, I would totally advocate for the field because it is growing. More and more companies and jobs are going to be created in this field in years to come. Also, make sure you get hands on experience. Most of this stuff is technical, that is, you need to know how to do things. The more experienced you are right out of the gate, the less your future employer has to train you, and the better you look as a candidate. As far as salary goes, I have a friend who got hired full time at a biopharma company before she even graduated. $24/hour with benefits, stocks, the whole shebang. Good luck!

While I do enjoy the technical aspects of it I have to say what attracts my the most is studying, researching and thinking about solutions. Do you think there's a good place for that in biotech or would I be better off somewhere else?

Of course! In my school we separate it into upstream and downstream. Downstream is the purification of a product, basically stuff for all the chemical engineers to do. Upstream deals with R&D, cell culture, genetic manipulation, things of that nature (generally). That's the stuff my friend is doing, and while they'll tell you there are less jobs in that area, the field is pretty inundated with chemical engineers, so you'd probably do fine. And there's loads of money being pumped into R&D, like billions of dollars.

For research, you'd also want to focus on getting experience in a research lab of some sort (preferably genetics, genetics is the future!), and would probably want to go to graduate school. Something like pharmacology would be an option, since that focuses on the research aspects of pharmaceuticals (if that's what you were interested in). I'm sure there is an analogous field for whatever flavor of biotechnology you are most interested in.
